77: 
78: ### Shared helper
79: 
80: `.chezmoitemplates/script-lib.sh` is included right after the shebang with `{{ template "script-lib.sh" "<script name>" }}`; it has no shebang of its own.
81: It holds no data beyond the script name: a script that needs data passes it to the function (`load_brew "{{ .brew.prefix }}"`), so a data change re-runs only the scripts that read it.
82: It provides:
83: 
84: - `set -euo pipefail`;
85: - `log` and `warn` (prefixed with the script name, to stderr);
86: - `have` (`command -v` wrapper);
87: - `run` (executes, or prints the command with `printf %q` when `CHEZMOI_SCRIPTS_DRY_RUN=1`; read-only queries are written without `run`, so they still execute);
88: - `as_root <why> <command...>` (logs why, then calls `run sudo`, or `run` directly when already root);
89: - `load_brew <prefix>` (gives the script the environment of the user's shell: it exports `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` with the default `~/.config` and evaluates `brew shellenv` from the prefix, which is the `brew.prefix` data, when `HOMEBREW_PREFIX` is not set, so that scripts after a first Homebrew install find the tools);
90: - `report_undeclared <what> <installed> <declared>` (lists installed names that are not declared, removes nothing);
91: - a warning when the dry-run variable is set while `CHEZMOI=1`.
92: 
93: `load_brew` exports `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` because Homebrew keeps its trust file in `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/homebrew` and looks in `~/.homebrew` when the variable is unset.
94: Without the file, third-party taps are untrusted and brew-file lists the 20 installed tap formulae of the Brewfile as missing (found with the live harness: `brew file install --dry-run` printed a `brew install` line for them in a bare environment, and printed nothing once `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` was set).
95: A shell that sourced `rc.d` has the variable, but ssh commands, cron and `env -i` do not.
96: `brew shellenv` prepends the Homebrew directory to `PATH` unconditionally, which is why the harness always passes `HOMEBREW_PREFIX` (so `load_brew` never evaluates it there) and refuses a script that embeds the real prefix when asked to leave it unset.
97: 
98: An edit to the helper changes every script that includes it, so each runs once more; all of them are no-ops on a provisioned machine.
99: 
100: ### No removals, and a drift report
101: 
102: Uninstalling stays a deliberate human action.
103: Each package script ends with a read-only report of what is installed and undeclared:
104: 
105: - brew: the `$ brew uninstall` and `$ brew untap` lines of `brew file clean --dry-run` (formulae and taps), plus `brew list --cask` minus the `cask` lines of the Brewfile; on Linux that lists every installed cask, `whosthere` today;
106: - pipx: `pipx list --short` minus the keys of `packages.json`;
107: - krew: `kubectl krew list` minus the combined plugin list, ignoring `krew` itself.
108: 
109: mise is not covered: `mise prune --dry-run` lists stale versions, not undeclared tools, so it stays with `rationalize-package-ownership`.
110: 
111: ### Brew script details
112: 
113: - It sources no `brew-wrap` and exports no brew-file variable: the config's `env` table passes `HOMEBREW_BREWFILE_BACKUP`, `FULL_NAME`, `LEAVES` and `ON_REQUEST`, and the Brewfile path defaults to `~/.config/brewfile/Brewfile`.
114:   `HOMEBREW_BREWFILE_TOP_PACKAGES` does not change the report on this machine (`gcc` is declared), so it is not exported either.
115: - Homebrew or brew-file counts as missing when `brew` is not found or `brew file version` fails; the script then runs brew-file's installer, which installs Homebrew first when needed and ends with `brew doctor`, failing the script when it reports a problem.
116:   Homebrew's installer calls sudo, and `NONINTERACTIVE=1` makes it use cached credentials and never prompt, so the script caches them first through `as_root` (`sudo -v`): the one place where a password prompt can appear, and it shows in the sudo log of the harness.
117:   Without a terminal and without passwordless sudo, `sudo -v` fails, and so does the script, before anything is installed.
118: - A missing deployed Brewfile fails the script: brew-file would create a Brewfile from the installed packages instead of installing anything.
119: - `rustup default stable` runs when `rustup default` does not report a default toolchain; a missing gh login is only warned about, because a login needs a terminal.
120: - The darwin branch is the `brew bundle` call of the old krew script, with a guard for a missing `brew`; its lists are the trigger.
121: ### Before scripts
122: 
123: - The prerequisites script renders empty unless the os-release `id` is `debian` or `id_like` names it (Ubuntu, Kali, Mint), and when `packages.linux.apt` is empty; chezmoi neither runs nor lists an empty script.
124:   It checks each package with `dpkg-query` and calls sudo, for `apt-get update` and one `apt-get install`, only when a package is missing.
125: - The decrypt script uses the binary that is applying, through `CHEZMOI_EXECUTABLE`, which chezmoi sets for every script it runs, and falls back to `chezmoi` on `PATH` when the script is run by hand.
126:   A path rendered into the script would change after every chezmoi upgrade and make the script pending again, and `PATH` may not hold chezmoi on a fresh machine.
127:   It writes the identity with umask 077, so the file is never group-readable, then `chmod 600` as before.
128: - The limits script reads `system.limits.nofile`, checks at render time that both values are whole numbers with `0 < soft <= hard`, and renders empty when the data is absent.
129:   It compares the file with the two wanted lines and exits when they match.
130:   When the file holds a higher or non-numeric limit it warns and leaves the file alone; otherwise it writes with `sudo install -m 0644 /dev/stdin`, so root owns the file and the mode is explicit.
131: 
132: ### Package manager scripts
133: 
134: - `11-mise`, `12-pipx`, `13-krew` and `21-vim-plugins` call `load_brew`, so they find their tools right after a first Homebrew install, and skip with a warning and exit 0 when the tool is absent: a machine without that manager still applies, at the cost that chezmoi then counts the script as run until its input changes.
135:   Only a missing input that the apply itself should have written (the deployed `packages.json`, the Brewfile, the vimrc and Vundle) fails the script.
136: - `12-pipx` compares `jq` keys of the deployed `packages.json` with `pipx list --short`, writes the filtered copy under `$XDG_CACHE_HOME` (inside `$HOME`, removed on exit) only when a venv is missing, and does not write it in dry-run mode.
137:   Its header comment holds the refresh command of `packages.json`.
138: - `13-krew` ignores `krew` itself and the `PLUGIN` header in `kubectl krew list`; a missing `kubectl krew` is a skip.
139: - `11-mise` has no input besides the deployed global config: `mise install --yes` leaves other versions alone and prunes nothing.
140: 
141: ### Krew per system
142: 
143: `.chezmoidata/packages.yaml` holds `packages.common.krews` (plugins that krew offers on Linux, macOS and Windows: explore, get-all, stern, tail), `packages.linux.krews` (colorize-managed-fields, neat, node-shell, which krew offers on Linux and macOS only) and `packages.darwin.krews`, empty until reviewed on a macOS machine (the three Linux plugins are available there).
144: The script's list is the shared list plus the list of the current system, without duplicates, sorted; on this laptop it is the same 7 plugins as before.
145: It renders empty on a system with no list, and on Windows, which would need a PowerShell script.
146: 
147: ### Vim plugins
148: 
149: The vim plugin script stays, now that Neovim is the editor, because it costs nothing and does nothing when the plugins are present; `vim.ycm_build` is false, and no YouCompleteMe build runs on request or by default.
150: The core library check is `ycm_core*.so` under `~/.vim/bundle/YouCompleteMe/third_party/ycmd/`.
151: The script needs the deployed vimrc and the Vundle external: when either is missing it fails, so that chezmoi runs it again.
152: A non-zero exit of vim is logged as a warning and does not fail the script.
153: `vim` runs with `-N` because Ex mode starts with `compatible` set, and Vundle's autoload file defines its commands over continuation lines that a compatible vim does not join.
154: The vimrc loads Vundle at line 21 and sets `nocompatible` only at line 665, so Vundle loads too early.
155: Without `-N` (measured on this machine with the real vimrc, `:command` listing after startup), `Plugin` and `PluginInstall` exist with an empty definition and vim exits 1: the vimrc declares no plugin and `+PluginInstall` does nothing, with only a warning from the script.
156: With `-N` both commands are complete and vim exits 0.
157: In an interactive vim the problem does not appear, because finding a vimrc resets `compatible` before it is read.
158: Moving `set nocompatible` to the top of the vimrc, as Vundle's documentation asks, would make `-N` unnecessary; editing the vimrc belongs to `cleanup-dead-config`.
159: `-n` and `-i NONE` keep vim from writing swap and viminfo files.
160: Removing Vundle and the `Plugin 'ycm-core/YouCompleteMe'` line of the vimrc belongs to `cleanup-dead-config`; until then a fresh machine prints a missing core library message when vim starts.
161: 
162: ### Data added to `.chezmoidata/packages.yaml`
163: 
164: - `packages.linux.apt`: the 12 packages of the prerequisites script (the empty `dpkgs` key is dropped).
165: - `packages.common.krews`, `packages.linux.krews`, `packages.darwin.krews` as above.
166: - `system.limits.nofile`: `soft: 32768`, `hard: 65536` (the live values on 2026-11-12; the script renders empty when the key is absent).
167: - `vim.ycm_build: false`.

- `brew.prefix: /home/linuxbrew/.linuxbrew`, the only place the Homebrew prefix is written in the scripts.

`home/dot_config/pipx/packages.json` is regenerated from `pipx list --json` (28 venvs: the 23 declared plus calcure, euporie, hike, ipython and pynvim).
All 23 existing entries change too, because their recorded app paths and versions no longer match.

The file holds no absolute path.
pipx writes `app_paths`, `man_paths`, `completion_paths` and their `_of_dependencies` forms after an install, and `pipx install-all` never reads them back: it installs the package at the recorded version, injects the recorded extras, and writes fresh metadata from the new venv.
The six fields stay in the file, emptied (`[]` or `{}`), because pipx requires `app_paths` and `app_paths_of_dependencies`.
`source_interpreter` is `null` for the same reason of portability: it was the Homebrew Python path, which does not exist on macOS or another prefix, and pipx prints a notice and uses its default Python when it is missing.
The cost is the Python pin: all 28 venvs run Python 3.13 today, and a venv built from this file uses pipx's default Python (3.14 on this machine).
`python_version` stays in the file as information; pipx does not use it to choose an interpreter.
`pipx install-all --python <path>` would pin one interpreter for the whole run; whether to pin, and with which data key, is left to `rationalize-package-ownership`.
The F24 part about user-specific paths is closed here for this file.

The file is refreshed with:

```sh
pipx list --json | jq --indent 4 '(.. | objects | select(has("app_paths"))) |= (.app_paths = [] | .app_paths_of_dependencies = {} | .man_paths = [] | .man_paths_of_dependencies = {} | .completion_paths = [] | .completion_paths_of_dependencies = {}) | .venvs[].metadata.source_interpreter = null'
```

It stays plain JSON, not a template: nothing in it depends on the machine.

## Risks / Trade-offs

- [Risk] Every script runs once on the next apply because its content changed or its name is new. → Each is a no-op on this machine by design; proved with the harness (isolated and live read-only modes) before the supervised apply.
- [Risk] Moving brew, pipx and mise to after-scripts means files that need those tools (templates calling `output` or `lookPath`) render before the tools exist on a fresh machine, and `add-mise-app-desktop-entries` writes its entries on the second apply. → Unchanged from today for this machine; a fresh machine is handled in `fresh-machine-bootstrap`, which may move only the brew bootstrap back to a before-script.
- [Risk] `pipx install-all` on a filtered file loses injected packages or Python pins. → Filter with `jq` on the `venvs` keys only, keeping each venv's full metadata.
- [Risk] Dropping `gh auth login` leaves a fresh machine without gh auth. → gh reads its token from the environment; the brew script logs a warning when `gh auth status` fails.
- [Risk] `CHEZMOI_SCRIPTS_DRY_RUN=1 chezmoi apply` runs the scripts in dry-run mode, and chezmoi records them as run because they exit 0, so the real apply later skips them. → The helper warns when both variables are set, `AGENTS.md` says to use the variable only on rendered scripts, and the harness never goes through `chezmoi apply`.
- [Risk] sudo asks for its password when a system change is needed, so apt and limits scripts cannot be fully non-interactive on a fresh machine. → That prompt is allowed by the spec; a provisioned machine never reaches it.
- [Risk] The vim plugin command cannot be proved without installing plugins. → The harness checks the call; the real run is part of the supervised apply, and the script only warns when vim fails.
- [Trade-off] The dry-run variable is a local convention, not a chezmoi feature; documented in `AGENTS.md`.
- [Trade-off] `brew file clean --dry-run` is parsed by line prefix, which ties the report to brew-file's output format; a format change makes the report empty rather than wrong, and the harness fixture catches it.

## Resolved questions

- Keep Vundle and the vim plugins, now that Neovim is the editor? Yes, without YouCompleteMe (decided 2026-11-12).
- Should the undeclared report cover more than brew? Yes: brew (formulae, taps, casks), pipx and krew, read-only; not mise (decided 2026-11-12).

## D1: vim

Under plain `vim -Es` (no `-N`) the repository vimrc defines the Vundle commands completely and exits 0. The old deployed vimrc still fails that check, which is why the script keeps `-N` too.

## D2: where the tools come from

| Tool | Declared in | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `jq` | mise config (`jq = "latest"`) | mise has it through aqua. `/usr/bin/jq` is only an accidental dependency of `clevis-luks` and `fwupd`. |
| `kubectl` | mise config (`kubectl = "latest"`) | as you said |
| `vim` | Brewfile (`brew vim`) | mise offers vim only as a conda package or a build-from-source plugin, so brew is the first practical choice. Override me if you want it in mise anyway. The design notes that Neovim is the main editor now. |

**Effects on this laptop, none applied:**
- **jq:** the next `mise install` installs `jq` 1.8.2. It's the only pending tool.
- **kubectl:**
  - The `latest` setting is already satisfied by the installed 1.36.0.
  - The mise shim comes before Homebrew in your `PATH`, so `kubectl` would move from Homebrew's 1.37.0 to mise's 1.36.0 until you run `mise upgrade kubectl` (1.37.2 is current).
  - I left `kubernetes-cli` in the Brewfile, since duplicate cleanup belongs to `rationalize-package-ownership`.
- **vim:**
  - It's installed here only as a dependency of `ttyd`.
  - I checked with `brew file init` into a scratch file: brew-file's next regeneration of the Brewfile would drop the `brew vim` line. A fresh machine is not affected.
  - Running `brew install vim` once would mark it as installed on request. I did not run it, since it's a brew install.

## Option D without its weakness

- **Why `lookPath` fails:** the original idea hashed whether the tool was on `PATH` at render time. An interactive shell and cron have different `PATH`s, so the hash would flip without any change on the machine.
- **What I did instead:**
  - A new `tools-present` template writes `# tools: pipx=present jq=present` into the script's hash comment.
  - It uses chezmoi's `findExecutable` over a fixed list of directories: the mise shims, `<brew.prefix>/bin`, `~/.local/bin`, `/usr/local/bin`, `/usr/bin` and `/bin`. It never reads the `PATH` of whoever renders.
- **How it behaves:**
  - A missing tool is a skip (warning, exit 0), so the apply continues.
  - Chezmoi records the hash with `absent`. When the tool appears in one of those directories, the next render changes, and `chezmoi status` shows the script as pending again.
  - `11-mise`, `12-pipx`, `13-krew` and `21-vim-plugins` use it. Two new helpers go with it: `need <tool>...`, and `load_mise`, which puts the mise shims first on `PATH` (mise > brew > distro).
- **Proof:**
  - The text flips when a tool file appears or disappears.
  - A non-executable file does not count.
  - The text is identical under `PATH=/nonexistent`, the normal `PATH`, and a `PATH` holding every tool in an unsearched directory.
  - The checks are not vacuous: a mutant with a constant "present" fails the flip checks, and a mutant using `lookPath` fails all four `PATH` checks.
  - An isolated test confirms a jq that exists only as a mise shim is found.
- **Residual limits (written in the design):**
  - A tool installed outside the listed directories does not re-run the script (the next input edit does).
  - A mise shim left by an uninstalled tool counts as present.
  - A custom mise data directory is not searched.

2. `feat(pkg:brew): declare vim, now installed only as a dependency` (only the Brewfile)
3. `fix(editor:vim): set nocompatible before Vundle loads` (only the vimrc)
4. `refactor(chezmoi:scripts): split the install script per package manager`, with this body:

   ```text
   Adds 10-brew, 11-mise, 12-pipx, 13-krew and 21-vim-plugins, the shared
   and per-system krew lists, and the load_mise, need and tools-present
   helpers. A script that skips for a missing tool runs again when the tool

   ```

   It contains the scripts, the helper changes, the `tools-present` template, `packages.yaml`, and the proposal, design, spec and tasks updates.

<!-- @generated by usage-cli from usage spec -->
# `mise reshim`

- **Usage:** `mise reshim [-f --force] [--system]`
- **Effect:** modifies state
- **Source code:** [`src/cli/reshim.rs`](https://github.com/jdx/mise/blob/main/src/cli/reshim.rs)

Create shims for executables provided by installed tools

Run this when an executable was added to an existing installation outside
mise, for example after a language package manager installed a CLI globally.
It rebuilds your shim directory (~/.local/share/mise/shims by default).
`--system` rebuilds the system shim directory used by `mise install --system`.

Shims are created for all installed versions. When invoked, a shim picks the
version to run from the current config. `--force` rebuilds mise-owned shims;
it does not turn unrelated files into mise-owned shims.
See <https://mise.jdx.dev/dev-tools/shims.html>

## Flags
- **`-f --force`** — Rebuild all mise-owned shims
- **`--system`** — Rebuild the system shims, for tools installed with `mise install --system`
- **`-h --help`** — Print help

## Examples

Rebuild shims, then run node through its shim

```
mise reshim
~/.local/share/mise/shims/node -v
v24.11.0
```

<!-- generated reference navigation -->

## Related documentation

- [Shims](/dev-tools/shims.html).
- [All commands](/cli/).
- [Global flags and argument syntax](/cli/#global-flags).

```

c() { # name mode fixture script flags exit sudo outre callsre
  local name=$1 mode=$2 fix=$3 script=$4 flags=$5 want_exit=$6 want_sudo=$7 outre=$8 callsre=$9
  local fixarg=() ok=1 why=''
  [ -n "$fix" ] && fixarg=(-f "$H/fix/$fix")
  # shellcheck disable=SC2086
  "$H/run.sh" -m "$mode" -n "$name" "${fixarg[@]}" $flags "$script" < /dev/null > "$H/out/last.txt" 2>&1
  local d=$H/out/logs/$name status sudo refused
  status=$(cat "$d/status" 2> /dev/null || echo '?')
  sudo=$(wc -l < "$d/sudo.log")
  refused=$(wc -l < "$d/refused.log")
  [ "$status" = "$want_exit" ] || { ok=0; why+=" exit=$status(want $want_exit)"; }
  [ "$sudo" = "$want_sudo" ] || { ok=0; why+=" sudo=$sudo(want $want_sudo)"; }
  if [ "$mode" = live ]; then [ "$refused" = 0 ] || { ok=0; why+=" refused=$refused"; }; fi
  if [ -n "$outre" ] && ! grep -q -E -- "$outre" "$d/out.log"; then ok=0; why+=" out!~/$outre/"; fi
  if [ -n "$callsre" ] && ! grep -q -E -- "$callsre" "$d/calls.log"; then ok=0; why+=" calls!~/$callsre/"; fi
  if [ "$ok" = 1 ]; then pass=$((pass + 1)); printf 'PASS  %-18s %s\n' "$name" "$mode"; else fail=$((fail + 1)); printf 'FAIL  %-18s %s%s\n' "$name" "$mode" "$why"; fi
}

# fixtures that the earlier ad-hoc runs did not need
mkdir -p -m 700 "$H/fix/prereq-ok"
printf '#!/bin/sh\nprintf "ii "\n' > "$H/fix/prereq-ok/dpkg-query"
chmod 700 "$H/fix/prereq-ok/dpkg-query"

# pipx-shim: pipx-missing plus a jq that exists only as a mise shim under the scratch home (found through load_mise)
rm -rf "$H/fix/pipx-shim"; cp -a "$H/fix/pipx-missing" "$H/fix/pipx-shim"
mkdir -p "$H/fix/pipx-shim~/share/mise/shims"
printf '#!/bin/sh\nexec /usr/bin/jq "$@"\n' > "$H/fix/pipx-shim~/share/mise/shims/jq"

**Exceptions decided by the user on 2026-11-12, after the plan-mode review:**

- The krew script has one branch per operating system, with a shared list and per-system lists, and the darwin `brew bundle` call moves to the brew script.
- `packages.json` is synchronized with the installed venvs, in its own commit.
- `TODO.md` entries are called items instead of lines, and two backlog entries are added, each in its own commit.

## Decisions

| `run_onchange_after_10-brew.sh.tmpl` | after | Brewfile (darwin: brews and casks) | Homebrew and brew-file if missing; `brew file install` against the deployed `~/.config/brewfile/Brewfile`; reports undeclared formulae, taps and casks; `rustup default stable` only when no default toolchain; warns when gh is not logged in; darwin branch: `brew bundle` |
| `run_onchange_after_11-mise.sh.tmpl` | after | `dot_config/mise/config.toml`, presence of `mise` | `mise install --yes` |
| `run_onchange_after_12-pipx.sh.tmpl` | after | `dot_config/pipx/packages.json`, presence of `pipx` and `jq` | installs only venvs missing from `pipx list --short`, through a filtered copy of the spec file; reports undeclared venvs |
| `run_onchange_after_13-krew.sh.tmpl` | after | the combined plugin list, presence of `kubectl` and `kubectl-krew` | Linux and macOS; installs only missing plugins; reports undeclared plugins; renders empty when the list is empty |
| `run_onchange_after_20-vscodium-extensions.sh.tmpl` | after | extension list | as today; `.vsix` skipped when its `publisher.name` is installed |
The bat hash covers the external declarations, not the upstream theme files, which the weekly refresh may change without re-running the script.
The `.vsix` directory is outside the repository, so adding a file there does not re-run the VSCodium script.

A script that skips when a tool is missing also hashes whether that tool is there.
Its hash comment holds `# tools: <tool>=present|absent ...`, produced by the `tools-present` template: for each tool, chezmoi's `findExecutable` looks in a fixed list of directories (the mise shims, `<brew.prefix>/bin`, `~/.local/bin`, `/usr/local/bin`, `/usr/bin`, `/bin`).
A skip exits 0, so chezmoi records it like a run, and the recorded hash holds `absent`; when the tool is installed in one of those directories the next render holds `present`, and the script runs again by itself.
The lookup never reads the `PATH` of the process that renders, which is what makes the plain `lookPath` version of this idea unreliable: an interactive shell, cron and `env -i` have different `PATH`s and would flip the hash without any change on the machine (the harness shows the text is identical under three different `PATH`s, and fails when `lookPath` is used instead).
Residual limits: a tool installed outside those directories does not re-run the script (the next edit of its input does), a mise shim left behind by an uninstalled tool counts as present, and a custom mise data directory is not searched.
The scripts put the same directories on their own `PATH` at run time (`load_brew`, `load_mise`), so what the render sees is what the script can use.

- `as_root <why> <command...>` (logs why, then calls `run sudo`, or `run` directly when already root);
- `load_brew <prefix>` (gives the script the environment of the user's shell: it exports `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` with the default `~/.config` and evaluates `brew shellenv` from the prefix, which is the `brew.prefix` data, when `HOMEBREW_PREFIX` is not set, so that scripts after a first Homebrew install find the tools);
- `load_mise` (puts the mise shims first on `PATH`, so that a mise tool wins over Homebrew and the distribution, and adds `~/.local/bin` last);
- `need <tool>...` (succeeds when every tool is found; otherwise warns, naming the missing ones, and fails, and the script ends with `need ... || exit 0`);
- `report_undeclared <what> <installed> <declared>` (lists installed names that are not declared, removes nothing);
### No removals, and a drift report

Uninstalling stays a deliberate human action.
Each package script ends with a read-only report of what is installed and undeclared:

- brew: the `$ brew uninstall` and `$ brew untap` lines of `brew file clean --dry-run` (formulae and taps), plus `brew list --cask` minus the `cask` lines of the Brewfile; on Linux that lists every installed cask, `whosthere` today;
- pipx: `pipx list --short` minus the keys of `packages.json`;
- krew: `kubectl krew list` minus the combined plugin list, ignoring `krew` itself.

mise is not covered: `mise prune --dry-run` lists stale versions, not undeclared tools, so it stays with `rationalize-package-ownership`.

### Package manager scripts

- `11-mise`, `12-pipx`, `13-krew` and `21-vim-plugins` call `load_brew` and `load_mise`, so they find their tools right after a first Homebrew or mise install, and `need` their tools.
  A missing tool is a skip (warning, exit 0), so that an apply never stops because an optional manager is absent, and the script runs again once the tool appears, because the tool's presence is part of its hash (see above).
  Only a missing input that the apply itself should have written (the deployed `packages.json`, the Brewfile, the vimrc and Vundle) fails the script, so that chezmoi retries it at the next apply.
- `12-pipx` compares `jq` keys of the deployed `packages.json` with `pipx list --short`, writes the filtered copy under `$XDG_CACHE_HOME` (inside `$HOME`, removed on exit) only when a venv is missing, and does not write it in dry-run mode.
  Its header comment holds the refresh command of `packages.json`.
- `13-krew` needs `kubectl` and `kubectl-krew` (the krew plugin manager, from the `krew` formula), ignores `krew` itself and the `PLUGIN` header in `kubectl krew list`, and skips when `kubectl krew version` fails.
- `11-mise` has no input besides the deployed global config: `mise install --yes` leaves other versions alone and prunes nothing.

### Tools the scripts need

Install priority is mise, then brew, then the distribution (`AGENTS.md`).
The scripts use a handful of tools, and each is declared once, by the highest-priority manager that offers it:

| Tool | Declared in | Why there |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `mise`, `pipx`, `krew` (the `kubectl-krew` plugin), `rustup`, `gh` | Brewfile | already there; the scripts only use them |
| `jq` | mise config (`jq = "latest"`) | the pipx script filters its spec file with it; mise has it through aqua; `/usr/bin/jq` on this laptop is an accidental dependency of other packages (`clevis-luks`, `fwupd`) and stays as a fallback |
| `kubectl` | mise config (`kubectl = "latest"`) | the krew script runs it; mise has it through aqua |
| `vim` | Brewfile (`brew vim`) | the vim plugin script runs it; mise offers vim only as a conda package or a build-from-source plugin, so brew is the first practical choice; it is a secondary editor now that Neovim is the main one |

Effects on this machine, none of them applied by this change:

- `mise install` will install `jq` (1.8.2 at the time of writing); `kubectl = "latest"` is already satisfied by the installed 1.36.0, since mise treats `latest` as the newest installed version until `mise upgrade`.
- The mise shim of `kubectl` comes before Homebrew in the interactive `PATH`, so `kubectl` moves from Homebrew's 1.37.0 to mise's 1.36.0 until `mise upgrade kubectl` (1.37.2 at the time of writing).
  The `kubernetes-cli` line stays in the Brewfile: removing duplicates between brew and mise is `rationalize-package-ownership`.
- `vim` is installed here only as a dependency of `ttyd`, and brew-file lists only packages installed on request, so its next regeneration of the Brewfile (after a brew command through `brew-wrap`) would drop the `brew vim` line (checked with `brew file init` into a scratch file: with the default settings `vim` is absent, with `vim` among the top packages it is listed).
  A fresh machine is not affected: `brew file install` installs `vim` on request.
  On this laptop, `brew install vim` once marks it as installed on request; it is the user's to run.

### Data added to `.chezmoidata/packages.yaml`

- `packages.linux.apt`: the 12 packages of the prerequisites script (the empty `dpkgs` key is dropped).
- `packages.common.krews`, `packages.linux.krews`, `packages.darwin.krews` as above.
- [Risk] `CHEZMOI_SCRIPTS_DRY_RUN=1 chezmoi apply` runs the scripts in dry-run mode, and chezmoi records them as run because they exit 0, so the real apply later skips them. → The helper warns when both variables are set, `AGENTS.md` says to use the variable only on rendered scripts, and the harness never goes through `chezmoi apply`.
- [Risk] sudo asks for its password when a system change is needed, so apt and limits scripts cannot be fully non-interactive on a fresh machine. → That prompt is allowed by the spec; a provisioned machine never reaches it.
- [Risk] A script skips because a tool is missing, and nobody notices. → The skip is a warning in the apply output, `chezmoi status` lists the script as pending again as soon as the tool appears in one of the searched directories, and the tools themselves are declared, so a missing one means an earlier step failed.
- [Risk] The tool presence is looked up in fixed directories while the script uses `PATH`. → `load_brew` and `load_mise` put the same directories on the script's `PATH`; the residual cases are listed with the hash line above.
- [Risk] The vim plugin command cannot be proved without installing plugins. → The harness checks the call; the real run is part of the supervised apply, and the script only warns when vim fails.
- [Trade-off] The dry-run variable is a local convention, not a chezmoi feature; documented in `AGENTS.md`.
- [Trade-off] `brew file clean --dry-run` is parsed by line prefix, which ties the report to brew-file's output format; a format change makes the report empty rather than wrong, and the harness fixture catches it.

## Done on the machine (your two yeses)

- **Deployed:** `~/.config/mise/config.toml`, `~/.config/brewfile/Brewfile` and `~/.config/vim/vimrc`, each as a single target with `--exclude=scripts`. I reviewed the diffs first: only the intended lines, plus the 664 to 640 mode change. The deployed vimrc now loads Vundle under plain `vim -Es`.
- **Installed:** `jq` 1.8.2 through `mise install jq`, run from `$HOME`. mise added the shim itself (137 to 138 shims), and `mise install --dry-run-code` now exits 0. Nothing else was installed, upgraded or removed, and the counts for brew, pipx, krew and VSCodium are unchanged.
- **Expected warning:** chezmoi now says "config file template has changed, run chezmoi init". I edited `.chezmoi.toml.tmpl` and did not run init, as the brief requires.

## Residual limit 1: configurable directories

- **Data and layers:**
  - `home/.chezmoidata/tools.yaml` holds `tools.search` with three layers: `dirs` (the default list), `extra` (searched after it) and `override` (replaces both when not empty).
  - Entries can be absolute, `~/x` or `<brew>/x`.
  - Bad entries fail the render with a message naming `tools.search`. Ten kinds are tested: relative, `~`, above home, a colon, a quote, a non-string and more.
- **Where you set it:**
  - Put local values in the local config, table `[data.tools.search]`. It wins over the data file, which I checked with a scratch config.
  - `chezmoi init` regenerates the config from the template, so hand-written values would have been dropped. The template now copies `extra` and `override` through. It prompts for nothing, and the two existing config-spec scenarios still hold.
  - This touches `.chezmoi.toml.tmpl`, which belongs to the archived `fix-chezmoi-config-template`. I recorded it as a small delta spec on `chezmoi-config` and listed it in the proposal.
- **Same list for search and run time:**
  - The `tools-present` template (the hash line) and the new `tools-use` template read the same list.
  - Scripts put those directories on their own `PATH` through `use_tool_dirs`. This replaces the `load_mise` I introduced last turn.
  - Rendered scripts now keep `~/` entries literal, so they hold no home path (the decrypt script still embeds the source dir, as before).
  - A change to the list re-runs the four scripts that read it, and nothing else.

## Residual limit 2: shim cleanup

- **What the step is:** `11-mise` now runs `mise reshim` after `mise install --yes`.
- **What mise's source says** (`src/shims.rs`): reshim adds missing shims and removes mise-owned shims that no installed tool provides. It leaves other files alone and does not touch tool versions. So it is not an uninstall; the spec's "never uninstall" requirement now says so.
- **How I proved it:**
  - **Sandbox:** the real mise binary runs offline in a scratch home with a fake `node` install, a stale shim, a current shim and a non-shim file. The stale shim is removed, the missing one is added, the others are kept, and a second run changes nothing.
  - **Preview on this laptop:** I ran mise against a symlink farm of the real installs and a copy of the real shims directory. A real reshim here would change nothing, with 137 shims before and after. Planting a stale shim in the copy gets it reported.
  - **Not run for real:** the real `mise reshim` was never executed here. In live mode the harness swaps it for `mise --version`.
- **What `mise uninstall` already does:** it rebuilds the shims itself. So the cleanup covers tools that vanished by other means, such as a deleted install directory.

## Something I caught in my own design

Scripts prepend the listed directories to `PATH`. With the real list that would put real `/usr/bin` and Homebrew's `bin` ahead of my stubs, and real tools could have run in an isolated test. I found it while wiring the harness, before any run. Isolated renders now use a scratch `tools.search.override`, and `run.sh` refuses an isolated script whose list holds a real directory (a test covers the refusal).

## Proof beyond the existing cases

Three mutants each fail the check meant to catch them: one that ignores the configured list, one that appends instead of prepending, and one that accepts relative entries. The harness now also runs shellcheck itself, because the final static pass found an SC2088 warning on the literal tilde that the harness runs didn't cover. It is fixed with an explicit directive.

listing=$(codium --list-extensions 2> /dev/null); then\n  warn \"codium --list-extensions failed: nothing is installed\"\n  exit 1\nfi\n# Extension ids are case-insensitive: compare in lower case.\ninstalled=$(printf '%s\\n' \"$listing\" | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]')\n\nfor ext in \"${extensions[@]}\"; do\n  if grep -qxF \"${ext,,}\" <<< \"$installed\"; then\n    continue\n  fi\n  log \"installing $ext\"\n  if run codium --install-extension \"$ext\"; then\n    installed+=$'\\n'\"${ext,,}\"\n  else\n    warn \"failed: $ext\"\n  fi\ndone\n\n# vsix_id <file>: the extension id (publisher.name) of a .vsix, from the package.json inside it;\n# without unzip or jq, or when the file is not a readable archive, the file name without its version suffix.\nvsix_id() {\n  local file=$1 id=''\n  if have unzip && have jq; then\n    id=$(unzip -p \"$file\" extension/package.json 2> /dev/null | jq -r 'select(.publisher and .name) | .publisher + \".\" + .name' 2> /dev/null || true)\n  fi\n  if [ -z \"$id\" ]; then\n    id=$(basename \"$file\" .vsix | sed -E 's/-[0-9]+(\\.[0-9A-Za-z+_@-]*)*$//')\n  fi\n  printf '%s' \"${id,,}\"\n}\n\n# Extensions that are not on Open VSX: .vsix files kept outside this repository.\n# A .vsix whose extension is already installed is skipped, whatever its version: upgrading it is a manual action.\nshopt -s nullglob\nfor vsix in \"$vsix_dir\"/*.vsix; do\n  id=$(vsix_id \"$vsix\")\n  if [ -z \"$id\" ]; then\n    warn \"$(basename \"$vsix\"): cannot tell which extension it holds, skipped\"\n    continue\n  fi\n  if grep -qxF \"$id\" <<< \"$installed\"; then\n    log \"$(basename \"$vsix\"): $id is installed, skipped\"\n    continue\n  fi\n  log \"installing $id from $vsix\"\n  if run codium --install-extension \"$vsix\"; then\n    installed+=$'\\n'\"$id\"\n  else\n    warn \"failed: $vsix\"\n  fi\ndone\n{{- end }}\n"

## Proposed commit 7

```text
fix(chezmoi:scripts): skip vsix files whose extension is installed
```

It changes 5 files: the script, the comment in `vscodium.yaml`, and `design.md`, `spec.md` and `tasks.md` (task 4.5 ticked).

- **Script**
  - **Helper and presence:** it uses the helper and the `codium` presence line like the other scripts, and the extensions are a quoted array.
  - **`.vsix` identification:**
    - A `.vsix` is identified by `publisher.name` from the archive's `package.json` (`unzip` and `jq`).
    - Without them, or if the file is not an archive, it uses the file name without its version suffix.
    - It is skipped when that id is installed, whatever the case or the version.
  - **Install list:** each install is added to the in-memory list, so nothing is installed twice.
  - **Failed install:** it is a warning and the script still exits 0, as today.
- **`vscodium.yaml:1`:** the comment named `modify_settings.json.tmpl`, which does not exist. It names `modify_settings.json` now (F27), and mentions the `.vsix` handling.
- **Behaviour change:** if `codium --list-extensions` fails, the script now exits 1 and installs nothing. Before, every extension would have looked missing and been reinstalled. Tell me if you would rather keep the old tolerance.

**Proof**
- **Isolated cases:**
  - There are 14, with real `.vsix` archives. They cover:
    - installed, missing and mixed-case ids;
    - the `package.json` id and the file-name fallback (one case is named differently from its id, with and without `jq`);
    - a corrupt archive, a dry run, `codium` absent, a failing listing, one failing install and no `.vsix` directory.
  - Install-call counts are asserted in each.
- **Live mode:** with the real `codium`, `unzip` and `jq`, the script exits 0 with no install call.
- **Mutant:** with the guard removed, three of the cases reinstall the `.vsix`.
- **Render checks:** `flip-codium` and `path-20` pass.
- **Static checks and validation:** shellcheck and `bash -n` are clean, and `openspec validate --strict` passes.
- **Machine state:** unchanged, still 71 extensions.

<skill_content name="openspec-verify-change">
# Skill: openspec-verify-change

Verify that an implementation matches the change artifacts (specs, tasks, design).

**Input**: Optionally specify a change name. If omitted, check if it can be inferred from conversation context. If vague or ambiguous you MUST prompt for available changes.

**Steps**

1. **If no change name provided, prompt for selection**

   Run `openspec list --json` to get available changes. Use the **AskUserQuestion tool** to let the user select.

   Show changes that have implementation tasks (tasks artifact exists).
   Include the schema used for each change if available.
   Mark changes with incomplete tasks as "(In Progress)".

   **IMPORTANT**: Do NOT guess or auto-select a change. Always let the user choose.

2. **Check status to understand the schema**
   ```bash
   openspec status --change "<name>" --json
   ```
   Parse the JSON to understand:
   - `schemaName`: The workflow being used (e.g., "spec-driven")
   - Which artifacts exist for this change

3. **Get the change directory and load artifacts**

   ```bash
   openspec instructions apply --change "<name>" --json
   ```

   This returns the change directory and context files. Read all available artifacts from `contextFiles`.

4. **Initialize verification report structure**

   Create a report structure with three dimensions:
   - **Completeness**: Track tasks and spec coverage
   - **Correctness**: Track requirement implementation and scenario coverage
   - **Coherence**: Track design adherence and pattern consistency

   Each dimension can have CRITICAL, WARNING, or SUGGESTION issues.

5. **Verify Completeness**

   **Task Completion**:
   - If tasks.md exists in contextFiles, read it
   - Parse checkboxes: `- [ ]` (incomplete) vs `- [x]` (complete)
   - Count complete vs total tasks
   - If incomplete tasks exist:
     - Add CRITICAL issue for each incomplete task
     - Recommendation: "Complete task: <description>" or "Mark as done if already implemented"

   **Spec Coverage**:
   - If delta specs exist in `openspec/changes/<name>/specs/`:
     - Extract all requirements (marked with "### Requirement:")
     - For each requirement:
       - Search codebase for keywords related to the requirement
       - Assess if implementation likely exists
     - If requirements appear unimplemented:
       - Add CRITICAL issue: "Requirement not found: <requirement name>"
       - Recommendation: "Implement requirement X: <description>"

6. **Verify Correctness**

   **Requirement Implementation Mapping**:
   - For each requirement from delta specs:
     - Search codebase for implementation evidence
     - If found, note file paths and line ranges
     - Assess if implementation matches requirement intent
     - If divergence detected:
       - Add WARNING: "Implementation may diverge from spec: <details>"
       - Recommendation: "Review <file>:<lines> against requirement X"

   **Scenario Coverage**:
   - For each scenario in delta specs (marked with "#### Scenario:"):
     - Check if conditions are handled in code
     - Check if tests exist covering the scenario
     - If scenario appears uncovered:
       - Add WARNING: "Scenario not covered: <scenario name>"
       - Recommendation: "Add test or implementation for scenario: <description>"

7. **Verify Coherence**

   **Design Adherence**:
   - If design.md exists in contextFiles:
     - Extract key decisions (look for sections like "Decision:", "Approach:", "Architecture:")
     - Verify implementation follows those decisions
     - If contradiction detected:
       - Add WARNING: "Design decision not followed: <decision>"
       - Recommendation: "Update implementation or revise design.md to match reality"
   - If no design.md: Skip design adherence check, note "No design.md to verify against"

   **Code Pattern Consistency**:
   - Review new code for consistency with project patterns
   - Check file naming, directory structure, coding style
   - If significant deviations found:
     - Add SUGGESTION: "Code pattern deviation: <details>"
     - Recommendation: "Consider following project pattern: <example>"

8. **Generate Verification Report**

   **Summary Scorecard**:
   ```
   ## Verification Report: <change-name>

   ### Summary
   | Dimension    | Status           |
   |--------------|------------------|
   | Completeness | X/Y tasks, N reqs|
   | Correctness  | M/N reqs covered |
   | Coherence    | Followed/Issues  |
   ```

   **Issues by Priority**:

   1. **CRITICAL** (Must fix before archive):
      - Incomplete tasks
      - Missing requirement implementations
      - Each with specific, actionable recommendation

   2. **WARNING** (Should fix):
      - Spec/design divergences
      - Missing scenario coverage
      - Each with specific recommendation

   3. **SUGGESTION** (Nice to fix):
      - Pattern inconsistencies
      - Minor improvements
      - Each with specific recommendation

   **Final Assessment**:
   - If CRITICAL issues: "X critical issue(s) found. Fix before archiving."
   - If only warnings: "No critical issues. Y warning(s) to consider. Ready for archive (with noted improvements)."
   - If all clear: "All checks passed. Ready for archive."

**Verification Heuristics**

- **Completeness**: Focus on objective checklist items (checkboxes, requirements list)
- **Correctness**: Use keyword search, file path analysis, reasonable inference - don't require perfect certainty
- **Coherence**: Look for glaring inconsistencies, don't nitpick style
- **False Positives**: When uncertain, prefer SUGGESTION over WARNING, WARNING over CRITICAL
- **Actionability**: Every issue must have a specific recommendation with file/line references where applicable

**Graceful Degradation**

- If only tasks.md exists: verify task completion only, skip spec/design checks
- If tasks + specs exist: verify completeness and correctness, skip design
- If full artifacts: verify all three dimensions
- Always note which checks were skipped and why

**Output Format**

Use clear markdown with:
- Table for summary scorecard
- Grouped lists for issues (CRITICAL/WARNING/SUGGESTION)
- Code references in format: `file.ts:123`
- Specific, actionable recommendations
- No vague suggestions like "consider reviewing"

Relative paths in this skill (e.g., scripts/, reference/) are relative to this base directory.
Note: file list is sampled.

</skill_content>

  - **Specs:** the change is moved to `archive/2026-11-12-make-install-scripts-idempotent`. The `install-scripts` spec is created with 14 requirements, and `chezmoi-config` gains one. I replaced the placeholder Purpose of the new spec and removed a duplicate modeline the archive tool left.
  - **Safety rule:** `AGENTS.md` has the approved wording.
  - **Tracking:** item 2 of `TODO.md` is ticked and row 4 of the audit's change map is set to "done, archived 2026-11-12". The audit's line 128, "avoided on purpose since 2026-10-26", is a dated status and stays as history.
- **Brief:** `d4f994e` fixes the verified scenarios and the commit list. `f3d1368` adds your five further exceptions and the list of actions done on this machine.
- **Brew:** no brew package was touched, so the brew hook committed nothing on `main`. I did not run `chezmoi init`, `chezmoi apply` or any install other than `mise install jq`.

## State of the machine

- **Changes (all approved):** four files were deployed as single targets:
  - mise config
  - Brewfile
  - vimrc
  - pipx `packages.json`

  `jq` 1.8.2 was installed with mise.
- **Counts:** 360 formulae, 1 cask, 140 mise tools, 28 pipx venvs, 7 krew plugins, 71 extensions and 138 shims. The limits file is unchanged, and the bat cache is still empty until the first apply.
- **Left for the supervised apply:** chezmoi lists 10 pending scripts. The real installs (`brew file install`, `pipx install-all`, krew, codium, Vundle, the Homebrew installer, apt) never ran. The harness proves each call and its guards, not the install itself.
- **Config template:** chezmoi warns that the config template changed (the `tools.search` pass-through). Run `chezmoi init` in a terminal when you choose; I did not.

## Frictions for the report

1. **Reporting channel:**
   - The agent name `chezmoi-orch` was lost after herdr restarts until you renamed the pane.
   - `herdr agent prompt` refuses a blocked agent (`agent_blocked`), so my verify report had to go through this pane.
   - My first report call returned no result type, and I had to check delivery separately.
2. **Tooling output:**
   - `openspec status --json` and `openspec instructions apply --json` print a "Loading change status..." line before the JSON, which breaks `jq`.
   - The `rtk` wrapper hid directory entries and filtered file listings, so I had to call `/bin/ls` directly.
   - The web fetch of the chezmoi docs returned thousands of navigation lines. The raw markdown from GitHub worked.
   - The read-only guard blocked `mise install --dry-run-code` (a false positive) and `export` of one variable.
3. **zsh and the shell:**
   - Two `<` redirections concatenate in zsh and keep only the last one in bash.
   - An unmatched glob aborts a whole zsh command.
   - The `shellcheck` and `yq` shims fail with "No version is set".
4. **Specs and process:**
   - The archive tool wrote a duplicate modeline and a "TBD" Purpose, and left a trailing blank line.
   - The brief names the wrong worktree path and has an ambiguous "line 2", both fixed before I started.
5. **Harness gaps I found myself:**
   - `brew shellenv` always puts the real brew ahead of the stubs.
   - brew-file calls `brew -v`, `python3` and `kubectl-krew` internally, so each needed an allow-list entry.
   - `-a vim` removed only the stub, so one isolated run executed the real `/usr/bin/vim` with the fixture vimrc and `-n -i NONE`. It ended with E492 and wrote nothing; I fixed the cause.
6. **A real `sudo true`:** one throwaway helper test ran outside the harness with a bare `PATH` and called the real `sudo true`. It failed at once with no password (stdin was `/dev/null`), so nothing changed. It may have left an authentication-failure line in the system log. The brief makes any real `sudo` a stop-and-ask.
